LESSON OBJECTIVE
Find the straight-line distance between any two points in the coordinate plane, including negative coordinates and missing coordinates.
WHAT YOU NEED TO KNOW
Horizontal and vertical coordinate changes form the legs of a right triangle. The segment joining the points is the hypotenuse, so the Pythagorean theorem gives its length.
KEY DEFINITIONS
An ordered pair (x, y) gives horizontal and vertical position. Δx means x₂−x₁, Δy means y₂−y₁, and distance is a nonnegative length measured in linear units.
CORE RULE
For A(x₁,y₁) and B(x₂,y₂), d=√[(x₂−x₁)²+(y₂−y₁)²]. The squared distance is d²=(Δx)²+(Δy)².
HOW IT WORKS
1. Write the two points in the same order. 2. Subtract x-coordinates and y-coordinates. 3. Square each difference and add. 4. Take the nonnegative square root; label the units.
WORKED EXAMPLE 1 — BASIC
A(0,0), B(3,4): Δx=3 and Δy=4. Thus d=√(3²+4²)=√25=5 units. Check: a 3–4–5 right triangle.
WORKED EXAMPLE 2 — NEGATIVE COORDINATES
A(−2,−1), B(4,7): Δx=4−(−2)=6, Δy=7−(−1)=8. Then d=√(36+64)=10 units; subtracting a negative increases the difference.
WORKED EXAMPLE 3 — HORIZONTAL AND VERTICAL
A(−2,3), B(4,3) share y=3, so d=|4−(−2)|=6. For A(5,−1), B(5,8), d=|8−(−1)|=9. The full formula gives the same results.
WORKED EXAMPLE 4 — EXACT RADICAL
A(−2,−3), B(5,4): Δx=7, Δy=7, so d=√(49+49)=√98=7√2 units. Do not round unless asked; squared distance is 98.
WORKED EXAMPLE 5 — MISSING COORDINATE
A(x,1), B(2,9), d=10 and x<2. Square: 100=(2−x)²+64, so (2−x)²=36. Hence 2−x=±6; x<2 selects 2−x=6, giving x=−4.
VERIFIED COORDINATE DIAGRAM

A(−2,−1), B(4,7), C(4,−1) make a right triangle. AC is 6 horizontal units, CB is 8 vertical units, and AB is 10 units by 6²+8²=10². Grid coordinates and segment lengths are generated at the same scale.
DESMOS STRATEGY

Enter: A=(−2,−1), B=(4,7), and sqrt((4−(−2))^2+(7−(−1))^2). Look for: points A and B and numerical result 10. Use it to answer: verify AB=10. Why it works: the expression applies the Pythagorean theorem to coordinate differences. Faster or not? Not for small integer coordinates; useful as a check with awkward values. Independent check: 6²+8²=100.
COMPARE WITHOUT ROOTS
To decide which segment is longer, compare d² values instead of computing square roots. Example: changes (8,6) give d²=100; changes (5,12) give d²=169, so the second is longer.
APPLICATIONS

A circle radius is the distance from its center to a point on the circle. A rectangle diagonal uses the same formula with width and height. For a triangle perimeter, calculate all three side lengths and add.
COMMON MISTAKES
Do not subtract an x from a y, forget parentheses around negative coordinates, omit the square root when asked for distance, or choose both signs when a missing coordinate has a stated inequality.
EXAM STRATEGY AND QUICK CHECK
Use squared distances to compare lengths; look for Pythagorean triples (3,4,5), (5,12,13), (8,15,17). Quick checks: (0,0) to (6,8) is 10; (−3,4) to (9,−1) is 13.
LESSON RECAP AND NEXT STEP

Distance=√[(Δx)²+(Δy)²], always nonnegative. Use exact radicals when needed; apply the formula to diagonals, radii, perimeters, and unknown coordinates. Continue to 18 practice problems, aligned answers, and the five-question test.
